learn: Parameters of distributions and of ML models; the IID assumption
Bayes' theorem: prior, likelihood, evidence, posterior
MLE recipe and derivations: linear regression (Gaussian noise → least squares), logistic regression (Bernoulli → log-loss), discrete PMF, Laplace noise (→ absolute error)
MAP estimation: brute-force MAP hypothesis and a continuous worked example
Most probable classification: Bayes optimal classifier and the Gibbs algorithm
Naïve Bayes: generative view, conditional independence, prediction rule, discrete training by counting, Laplace and m-estimate smoothing
Gaussian Naïve Bayes, mixed features, text classification with the multinomial model (two worked examples)
Naïve Bayes vs logistic regression; features and practical issues of Bayesian learning
intro.why: Probabilistic modelling justifies the loss functions of regression and classification, explains regularisation as a prior, and underlies generative models, Bayesian deep learning and language-model scoring.

sections.title: Bayesian learning and parameter estimation
sections.body: The session answers two questions left open earlier (p.3): where does logistic regression's cost come from, and why is the least-squares cost a reasonable choice for linear regression? The car table (p.4) can be read as raw numbers, as ordinal categories (Less/Neutral/More; Low/Medium/High) or as a mix, each implying a different distribution. A distribution = model + parameter θ; θ can be a vector, e.g. a normal distribution's θ = (mean, SD), estimated from the data $(x_i,P(x_i))$ (p.5).

sections.title: Parameters in ML models; MLE vs MAP
sections.plain: Regression coefficients are distribution parameters too.
sections.body:
Regression: CarPrice $=8.5+0.5\,$Mileage$-1.5\,$Mileage² has parameters $(\theta_0,\theta_1,\theta_2)$; classification wraps the same form in a sigmoid, CarPrice $=1/(1+e^{-(8.5+0.5M-1.5M^2)})$ (p.6). Model (p.7): $y^{(i)}=\theta^Tx^{(i)}+\varepsilon^{(i)}$, $\varepsilon^{(i)}\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)$.

Assumption: data are IID samples $X_1..X_n$, all independent with the same PMF (discrete) or PDF (continuous) $f(X\mid\theta)$: the likelihood of different values of $X$ depends on θ.

MLEMAP
Select θ that makes the observed data most likely: maximise $f(X_1,\dots,X_n\mid\theta)$Choose the θ that is most likely given the data: maximise $f(\theta\mid X_1,\dots,X_n)$

sections.title: Bayes' theorem
sections.body:
$$P(\theta\mid\text{data})=\frac{P(\text{data}\mid\theta)\,P(\theta)}{P(\text{data})},\qquad P(h\mid D)=\frac{P(D\mid h)P(h)}{P(D)}.$$

$P(h)$: prior probability of hypothesis $h$ (belief before seeing data, a distribution over θ); $P(D)$: prior probability of the training data (evidence); $P(D\mid h)$: probability of the data given $h$ (the likelihood $L(\theta)$); $P(h\mid D)$: posterior belief after seeing the data. MAP works with the left side, MLE with $P(D\mid h)$ only (p.8).

sections.title: The MLE recipe
sections.body:
1. Determine the formula for $LL(\theta)=\log\prod_if(X_i\mid\theta)=\sum_i\log f(X_i\mid\theta)$.
  2. Differentiate $LL(\theta)$ with respect to each θ.
  3. Solve (set to zero analytically, or use gradient ascent when no closed form exists).

Taking logs is safe because log is monotonic ($\hat\theta=\arg\max L=\arg\max LL$, illustrated on p.11 with $f(x)$ and $\log f(x)$ peaking at the same $x$); it turns products into sums and avoids numerical underflow. MLE answers: for which parameter value does the observed data have the largest probability?

sections.title: MLE for linear regression: least squares
sections.plain: Gaussian noise ⇒ maximise LL ⇔ minimise squared error.
sections.body:
Noise $p(\varepsilon^{(i)})=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}\exp(-\frac{(\varepsilon^{(i)})^2}{2\sigma^2})$, so each target is normal around the true value (p.10): $y^{(i)}\mid x^{(i)};\theta\sim\mathcal N(\theta^Tx^{(i)},\sigma^2)$,

$$p(y^{(i)}\mid x^{(i)};\theta)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}\exp\Big(-\frac{(y^{(i)}-\theta^Tx^{(i)})^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big).$$

Likelihood (p.11–12) $L(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^np(y^{(i)}\mid x^{(i)};\theta)$ and

$$LL(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n\log\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}\exp\Big(-\frac{(y^{(i)}-\theta^Tx^{(i)})^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big)=n\log\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}-\frac1{\sigma^2}\cdot\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n(y^{(i)}-\theta^Tx^{(i)})^2.$$

The first term doesn't depend on θ, and $1/\sigma^2>0$ just scales (p.13), so (p.14)

$$\hat\theta=\arg\max_\theta\Big(-\tfrac12\sum_i(y^{(i)}-\theta^Tx^{(i)})^2\Big)=\arg\min_\theta\ \tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^n(y^{(i)}-\theta^Tx^{(i)})^2.$$

With probabilistic assumptions on the data, least-squares regression corresponds to finding the MLE of θ. Maximising over σ as well gives $\hat\sigma^2=\frac1n\sum(y^{(i)}-\hat\theta^Tx^{(i)})^2$.

sections.title: MLE for logistic regression: cross-entropy
sections.body:
$y_i\mid x_i\sim\text{Bern}(\sigma(\theta^Tx_i))$ (p.15): $P_\theta(Y=1\mid X=x)=h_\theta(x)=\frac1{1+e^{-\theta^Tx}}$, $P_\theta(Y=0\mid X=x)=1-h_\theta(x)=\frac{e^{-\theta^Tx}}{1+e^{-\theta^Tx}}$; compactly $p(y\mid x;\theta)=h_\theta(x)^y(1-h_\theta(x))^{1-y}$ (the Bernoulli PMF $p^{x}(1-p)^{1-x}$).

$$L(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n\sigma(\theta^Tx^{(i)})^{y^{(i)}}\big[1-\sigma(\theta^Tx^{(i)})\big]^{1-y^{(i)}},\quad LL(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^ny^{(i)}\log\sigma(\theta^Tx^{(i)})+(1-y^{(i)})\log\big[1-\sigma(\theta^Tx^{(i)})\big].$$

Differentiate one term (p.16) using $\sigma'=\sigma(1-\sigma)$:

$$\frac{\partial LL}{\partial\theta_j}=\Big[\frac{y}{\sigma(\theta^Tx)}-\frac{1-y}{1-\sigma(\theta^Tx)}\Big]\sigma(\theta^Tx)[1-\sigma(\theta^Tx)]x_j=\big[y-\sigma(\theta^Tx)\big]x_j,\qquad \frac{\partial LL}{\partial\theta_j}=\sum_{i=1}^n\big[y^{(i)}-\sigma(\theta^Tx^{(i)})\big]x_j^{(i)}.$$

No closed form: solve by gradient ascent $\theta:=\theta+\alpha\nabla_\theta LL(\theta)$ (p.16–17). Maximising $LL$ is minimising the cross-entropy cost of Module 4.

sections.title: MLE summary
sections.body: For $n$ IID random variables from $f(X_i\mid\theta)$: $L(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^nf(X_i\mid\theta)$, $\hat\theta=\arg\max_\theta L(\theta)$, $LL(\theta)=\log L(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n\log f(X_i\mid\theta)$, and $$\theta_{MLE}=\arg\max_\theta LL(\theta).$$

sections.title: Additional problem: MLE for a discrete PMF
sections.body:
Example 1 (p.20): $X\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ with $P(0)=2\theta/3$, $P(1)=\theta/3$, $P(2)=2(1-\theta)/3$, $P(3)=(1-\theta)/3$, $0\le\theta\le1$. Ten independent observations: (3, 0, 2, 1, 3, 2, 1, 0, 2, 1). Counts: 0 → 2, 1 → 3, 2 → 3, 3 → 2.

$$L(\theta)=\Big(\frac{1-\theta}{3}\Big)^2\Big(\frac{2\theta}{3}\Big)^2\Big(\frac{2(1-\theta)}{3}\Big)^3\Big(\frac{\theta}{3}\Big)^3\ \ (\text{p.21})$$ $$LL(\theta)=2\log\frac{1-\theta}{3}+2\log\frac{2\theta}{3}+3\log\frac{2(1-\theta)}{3}+3\log\frac\theta3,\qquad \frac{dLL}{d\theta}=-\frac{2}{1-\theta}+\frac2\theta-\frac{3}{1-\theta}+\frac3\theta=\frac{-10\theta+5}{(1-\theta)\theta}=0\Rightarrow\hat\theta=0.5.$$

(The slide's second log line writes "$\cdot\log(\theta/3)^3$" where "+" is meant; the next line is correct.)

sections.title: Exercise: Laplace noise gives absolute error
sections.body:
Outputs $y_i=f(x_i)+e_i$ with Laplacian noise $f(y_i\mid\theta)=\frac1{2\theta}e^{-|y_i-\mu|/\theta}$, model $h(x_i)=\sum_i\theta_ix_i$, $\mu=h(x_i)$ (p.23).

$$L=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac1{2\theta}e^{-|y_i-\mu|/\theta},\qquad LL=-n\ln(2\theta)-\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{|y_i-\mu|}{\theta}\ \Rightarrow\ \arg\min\ n\ln(2\theta)+\sum_i\frac{|y_i-\mu|}{\theta}.$$

Gradient wrt the scale: $\frac n\theta-\frac{\sum|y_i-\mu|}{\theta^2}=0\Rightarrow\hat\theta=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n|y_i-\mu|$ (p.24). For the regression weights, maximising LL means minimising $\sum|y_i-h(x_i)|$: instead of MSE, MAE is the maximum-likelihood loss under Laplace noise (robust to outliers; the fitted line tracks the conditional median).

sections.title: Maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation
sections.body:
$$\theta_{MAP}=\arg\max_\theta f(\theta\mid X_1,\dots,X_n),\qquad h_{MAP}=\arg\max_{h\in H}P(h\mid D)=\arg\max_{h\in H}\frac{P(D\mid h)P(h)}{P(D)}=\arg\max_{h\in H}P(D\mid h)P(h).$$

Brute-force MAP (p.25): (1) determine the prior of each hypothesis; (2) compute the posterior for every distinct prior/hypothesis; (3) choose the highest. Continuous MAP (p.26): find the prior, derive the posterior, differentiate with respect to each θ, solve. The MAP estimator is the value of θ maximising the posterior; best hypothesis ≈ most probable hypothesis. In log form, $\theta_{MAP}=\arg\max[LL(\theta)+\log P(\theta)]$: a Gaussian prior on weights gives L2 (ridge) regularisation, a Laplace prior gives L1 (lasso).

sections.title: MAP worked example
sections.body:
Prior $f(x)=2x$ for $0\le x\le1$ (0 otherwise); likelihood $p(Y=y\mid X=x)=x(1-x)^{y-1}$ (geometric). Find the MAP estimate of $X$ given $Y=3$:

$$h_{MAP}\propto P(Y=3\mid X)P(X)=x(1-x)^2\cdot2x=2x^2-4x^3+2x^4,\qquad \frac{d}{dx}=4x-12x^2+8x^3=4x(1-x)(1-2x)=0\Rightarrow x\in\{0,0.5,1\}.$$

Values: $P(X\mid Y=3)\propto\{0,\ 0.125,\ 0\}$ → $x_{MAP}=0.5$ (p.28). (The unnormalised value 0.125 is not a probability; normalising by $\int_0^12x^2(1-x)^2dx=1/15$ gives density 1.875 at the mode.) The MLE alone, $\arg\max x(1-x)^2$, is $x=1/3$: the prior pulls the estimate up.

sections.title: Most probable classification of new instances
sections.plain: h_MAP(x) is not necessarily the most probable label.
sections.body: So far we found the most probable hypothesis $h_{MAP}$. Given a new instance $x$, what is its most probable classification? $h_{MAP}(x)$ is not necessarily it. Consider $P(h_1\mid D)=0.4$, $P(h_2\mid D)=0.3$, $P(h_3\mid D)=0.3$ with $h_1(x)=+$, $h_2(x)=-$, $h_3(x)=-$; $h_{MAP}=h_1$ predicts $+$, but the total posterior mass voting $-$ is 0.6.

sections.title: The Bayesian ML setting
sections.body: Bayesian analysis (p.30): start with a belief about the system (prior); obtain data and update the belief; the outcome is the posterior; with more data the old posterior becomes the new prior and the cycle repeats. $P(h\mid D)$ determines the class label. MLE and MAP are the same if the prior is uniform. This forms the basis for the Naïve Bayes classifier.

sections.title: Bayes optimal classifier
sections.plain: Average every hypothesis's vote by its posterior.
sections.body:
The most probable classification combines the predictions of all hypotheses weighted by their posteriors (p.31). For a value $v_j\in V$:

$$P(v_j\mid D)=\sum_{h_i\in H}P(v_j\mid h_i)P(h_i\mid D),\qquad v_{OB}=\arg\max_{v_j\in V}\sum_{h_i\in H}P(v_j\mid h_i)P(h_i\mid D).$$

Example 1 (p.32): $P(h_1\mid D)=.4$, $P(-\mid h_1)=0$, $P(+\mid h_1)=1$; $P(h_2\mid D)=.3$, $P(-\mid h_2)=1$, $P(+\mid h_2)=0$; $P(h_3\mid D)=.3$, $P(-\mid h_3)=1$, $P(+\mid h_3)=0$. Therefore $\sum P(+\mid h_i)P(h_i\mid D)=0.4$ and $\sum P(-\mid h_i)P(h_i\mid D)=0.6$, so the Bayes optimal classification is $-$. No other classifier using the same hypothesis space and prior can outperform it on average.

sections.title: Gibbs classifier
sections.plain: Sample one h by posterior; error ≤ 2× Bayes optimal.
sections.body: The Bayes optimal classifier is best but expensive with many hypotheses. Gibbs algorithm: choose one hypothesis at random according to $P(h\mid D)$; use it to classify the new instance. Under certain conditions (target drawn from the prior), $$E[\text{error}_{Gibbs}]\le2\,E[\text{error}_{BayesOptimal}].$$ With a correct uniform prior over $H$, pick any hypothesis from the version space uniformly; its expected error is no worse than twice Bayes optimal.

sections.title: Parameter estimation summary
sections.plain: IID; MLE vs MAP; large samples; uniform priors.
sections.body: Assumptions: IID samples with the same PMF/PDF $f(X\mid\theta)$; parameters such as $(\theta_0,\theta_1,\theta_2)$ estimated from data. MLE maximises $f(X_1..X_n\mid\theta)$; MAP maximises $f(\theta\mid X_1..X_n)$. If the sample is large, MLE yields an excellent estimator (consistent, asymptotically efficient). When no prior information is available, all hypotheses are equally likely, $p(h_i)=p(h_j)$, and MAP reduces to MLE.

sections.title: Naïve Bayes as a generative model
sections.body: Decision theory refresher (p.36): $$P(Y\mid X_1X_2\cdots X_n)=\frac{P(X_1X_2\cdots X_d\mid Y)P(Y)}{P(X_1X_2\cdots X_d)},\qquad P(c\mid x)=\frac{P(x\mid c)P(c)}{P(x)}$$ (posterior = likelihood × class prior / predictor prior), and with the naïve assumption $P(c\mid X)\propto P(x_1\mid c)P(x_2\mid c)\cdots P(x_n\mid c)P(c)$. These are generative models: by sampling from them one can generate synthetic data points in the input space (Gaussians, Naïve Bayes, mixtures of multinomials, mixtures of Gaussians, Bayesian networks).

sections.title: Applications; digit recognition
sections.body: Applications (p.37): categorising news, email spam detection, face recognition, sentiment analysis. Digit recognition (p.38): $X_1,\dots,X_n\in\{0,1\}$ (black vs white pixels), $Y\in\{5,6\}$.

sections.title: Generative classification and the Bayes classifier
sections.body: $p(y\mid x)=\frac{p(x\mid y)p(y)}{p(x)}$; for binary classification $p(x)=p(x\mid y=1)p(y=1)+p(x\mid y=0)p(y=0)$. For prediction the denominator is not needed (p.39): $$\arg\max_yp(y\mid x)=\arg\max_y\frac{p(x\mid y)p(y)}{p(x)}=\arg\max_yp(x\mid y)p(y).$$ The Bayes classifier for digits (p.40): $P(Y=5\mid X_1..X_n)=\frac{P(X\mid Y=5)P(Y=5)}{P(X\mid Y=5)P(Y=5)+P(X\mid Y=6)P(Y=6)}$ and similarly for 6; predict whichever is greater. Without assumptions, $P(X_1..X_n\mid Y)$ for $n$ binary pixels needs $2(2^n-1)$ parameters.

sections.title: The conditional independence assumption
sections.body: Naïve Bayes assumes the $X_i$ are conditionally independent given $Y$: $P(X_1\mid X_2,Y)=P(X_1\mid Y)$, and in general $$P(X_1,\dots,X_n\mid Y)=\prod_{j=1}^nP(X_j\mid Y),$$ i.e. $X_i$ and $X_j$ are conditionally independent given $Y$ for $i\ne j$. Parameters drop from $2(2^n-1)$ to $2n$ for binary features.

sections.title: Naïve Bayes prediction rule
sections.body:
$$P(Y=y_k\mid X_1..X_n)=\frac{P(Y=y_k)\prod_iP(X_i\mid Y=y_k)}{\sum_jP(Y=y_j)\prod_iP(X_i\mid Y=y_j)},\qquad \hat Y\leftarrow\arg\max_{y_k}\underbrace{P(Y=y_k)}_{\text{prior}}\prod_i\underbrace{P(X_i\mid Y=y_k)}_{\text{likelihood}}.$$

In practice sum logs, $\arg\max_k[\log\pi_k+\sum_i\log\theta_{ik}]$, to avoid underflow.

sections.title: Worked example: Play Tennis (EnjoySport)
sections.body:
Seven days with Sky, AirTemp, Humidity, Wind, Forecast → EnjoySport (3 Yes, 4 No). $P(Y)\sim$ Bernoulli, each $X_i\mid Y$ categorical (p.43). Learning (p.44), MLEs $\hat\theta_{ijk}=\frac{\#D\{X_i=x_{ij}\wedge Y=y_k\}}{\#D\{Y=y_k\}}$, $\hat\pi_k=\frac{\#D\{Y=y_k\}}{|D|}$:

ValueYesNoValueYesNo
Sunny3/32/4Strong2/33/4
Rainy0/32/4Breeze1/31/4
Hot0/31/4Same2/32/4
Warm3/31/4Change1/32/4
Cold0/32/4High1/33/4
Normal2/31/4

Testing (p.45), new day $X$ = (Sunny, Warm, Normal, Strong, Change):

$$P(\text{Yes}\mid X)\propto\tfrac33\cdot\tfrac33\cdot\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac37=0.0635,\qquad P(\text{No}\mid X)\propto\tfrac24\cdot\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac34\cdot\tfrac24\cdot\tfrac47=0.0067.$$

Yes > No → EnjoySport = Yes (normalised posterior 0.905).

sections.title: Naïve Bayes algorithm (discrete features)
sections.plain: Estimate π and θ by counting; classify by argmax.
sections.body:
TRAIN(examples):
  for each value y_k:  π_k ← #(Y = y_k) / |D|
     for each value x_ij of each attribute X_i:
        θ_ijk ← #(X_i = x_ij ∧ Y = y_k) / #(Y = y_k)      // + smoothing
CLASSIFY(x_new):
  return argmax_k  π_k · Π_i θ_ijk   where x_ij = x_new,i  // use log-sums in practice

Training is one pass over the data, $O(nd)$; prediction is $O(Kd)$ for $K$ classes.

sections.title: The zero-probability problem
sections.plain: One zero count kills the product.
sections.body: Second test day (p.47): $X$ = (Rainy, Warm, Normal, Breeze, Same). $P(\text{Yes}\mid X)\propto\frac03\cdot\frac33\cdot\frac23\cdot\frac13\cdot\frac23\cdot\frac37=0$ because Rainy never occurred on a Yes day, so No wins (0.00223) regardless of the other attributes. If one of the conditional probabilities is zero, the entire expression becomes zero (p.49). Smoothing is a technique for categorical data: a small-sample correction (pseudo-count) is incorporated in every estimate so no probability is zero.

sections.title: Laplace smoothing and the m-estimate
sections.body:
$$\text{Original: }P(A_i\mid C)=\frac{N_{ic}}{N_c},\qquad \text{Laplace: }P(A_i\mid C)=\frac{N_{ic}+1}{N_c+d},\qquad m\text{-estimate: }P(A_i\mid C)=\frac{N_{ic}+mp}{N_c+m}$$

$d$: number of distinct values of the attribute; $N_c$: instances in the class; $N_{ic}$: instances with value $A_i$ in class $c$; $p$: prior probability (of the value); $m$: equivalent sample size, how heavily to weight $p$ relative to the observed data (p.50; the m-estimate is the Bayesian approach). General additive smoothing $\hat\theta_i=\frac{x_i+\alpha}{N+\alpha d}$, with $\alpha=1$ for Laplace (p.51).

Second test day smoothed (p.52):

$$\text{Yes}:\ \tfrac{0+1}{3+2}\cdot\tfrac{3+1}{3+3}\cdot\tfrac{2+1}{3+2}\cdot\tfrac{1+1}{3+2}\cdot\tfrac{2+1}{3+2}\cdot\tfrac37=\tfrac15\cdot\tfrac46\cdot\tfrac35\cdot\tfrac25\cdot\tfrac35\cdot\tfrac37=0.00823$$$$\text{No}:\ \tfrac36\cdot\tfrac27\cdot\tfrac26\cdot\tfrac26\cdot\tfrac36\cdot\tfrac47=0.00454\ \Rightarrow\ \text{EnjoySport = Yes}.$$

Smoothing reverses the decision: the single zero no longer dominates. (Priors are left unsmoothed, as on the slides.)

sections.title: Continuous features and the Gaussian distribution
sections.body:
For continuous $X_i$ (p.53): $Y=\arg\max_yP(Y=y)\prod_iP(X_i\mid Y=y)$ with the assumption that $P(X_i\mid Y)$ is Gaussian. The normal pdf (p.54), mean = median = mode = μ, 68% of area within ±1σ:

$$p(x)=\frac1{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}},\quad-\infty\le x\le\infty.$$

Note that $p(x)$ is a density (can exceed 1); using it in the product is fine because the same $dx$ factor appears for every class.

sections.title: Gaussian NB: learning and prediction
sections.plain: Per-class mean and variance for each feature.
sections.body:
For each class (p.55): $P(Y=y_k)=$ instances of $y_k$ / total; for each attribute estimate the class-conditional mean and variance; classify by $\hat Y\leftarrow\arg\max_{y_k}P(Y=y_k)\prod_iP(X_i\mid Y=y_k)$. Training (p.56): $\mu_i=E[X_i\mid Y=y]$, $\sigma_i^2=E[(X_i-\mu_i)^2\mid Y=y]$.

Example (p.57), rows $(2,3,1,1)$, $(-1.2,2,0.4,1)$, $(1.2,0.3,0,0)$, $(2.2,1.1,0,1)$ for $(X_1,X_2,X_3,Y)$: $$\mu_1=E[X_1\mid Y=1]=\frac{2+(-1.2)+2.2}{3}=1,\qquad \sigma_1^2=\frac{(2-1)^2+(-1.2-1)^2+(2.2-1)^2}{3}=2.43.$$ (MLE uses $1/n$; the unbiased estimate divides by $n-1$, giving 3.64.)

sections.title: Mixed features: Play Tennis with numeric humidity
sections.body:
Humidity is now numeric (Yes: 85, 83, 85; No: 80, 70, 90, 50); test day (Humidity 60, Warm, Rainy, Breeze, Same). Yes: $\mu=84.33$, spread 1.15; No: $\mu=72.5$, spread 17.08 (these are sample standard deviations, labelled "σ²" on the slide; the variances are 1.33 and 291.67).

$$P(\text{Yes}\mid X)\propto P(\text{Rainy}|Y)P(\text{Warm}|Y)\,\mathcal N(60;84.33,1.15)\,P(\text{Breeze}|Y)P(\text{Same}|Y)\tfrac37=\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac33\cdot\mathcal N\cdot\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac37$$

with $\mathcal N(60;84.33,1.15)\approx1.3\times10^{-97}$ (60 is 21 standard deviations away), while $\mathcal N(60;72.5,17.08)=0.0179$. So No wins by a huge margin. Tiny densities like this are why implementations work with log-probabilities.

sections.title: Exercise: Pass/Fail with hours and gender
sections.body:
Data (p.59): Pass: (4.5, M), (7, F), (8, F), (9, M); Fail: (2, M), (4, F), (2.5, M), (3, F), (8.3, M). Test: hours 3.5, male. Priors $4/9=0.44$, $5/9=0.56$. With sample SDs: Pass $\mu=7.125$, $s=1.931$, $\mathcal N(3.5)=0.0355$; Fail $\mu=3.96$, $s=2.536$, $\mathcal N(3.5)=0.1547$.

$$P(\text{Pass}\mid X)\propto\tfrac24\cdot0.0355\cdot0.44=0.0079,\qquad P(\text{Fail}\mid X)\propto\tfrac35\cdot0.1547\cdot0.56=0.0516\ \Rightarrow\ \text{Fail}.$$

The slide's partial solution uses $P(3.5\mid\text{Pass})=0.1056$, which we could not reproduce (see flags); the decision is Fail either way.

sections.title: Text classification: bag of words
sections.body: A document is represented by its word counts (p.62): e.g. a movie review becomes {it: 6, I: 5, the: 4, to: 3, and: 3, seen: 2, yet: 1, would: 1, whimsical: 1, …}. Word order and grammar are discarded; the multinomial model treats the document as $n$ independent draws of words from a class-specific distribution.

sections.title: Multinomial NB example: "A very close game"
sections.body:
Training (p.63): "A great game" (Sports), "The election was over" (Not), "Very clean match" (Sports), "A clean but forgettable game" (Sports), "It was a close election" (Not). $P(\text{Sports})=3/5$, $P(\text{Not})=2/5$; Sports has 11 words, Not has 9; vocabulary $|V|=14$. Unsmoothed: $P(X\mid\text{Sports})=\frac2{11}\cdot\frac1{11}\cdot\frac0{11}\cdot\frac2{11}=0$ because "close" never appears in Sports.

Laplace (p.64–66): add 1 to every count and $|V|=14$ to the divisor, so the division never exceeds 1 and $P(\text{close}\mid\text{sports})\ne0$.

wordP(word | Sports)P(word | Not sports)
a(2+1)/(11+14)(1+1)/(9+14)
very(1+1)/(11+14)(0+1)/(9+14)
close(0+1)/(11+14)(1+1)/(9+14)
game(2+1)/(11+14)(0+1)/(9+14)
$$P(\text{Sports})\prod=\tfrac{3}{25}\cdot\tfrac{2}{25}\cdot\tfrac{1}{25}\cdot\tfrac{3}{25}\cdot\tfrac35=2.76\times10^{-5},\qquad P(\text{Not})\prod=\tfrac{2}{23}\cdot\tfrac{1}{23}\cdot\tfrac{2}{23}\cdot\tfrac{1}{23}\cdot\tfrac25=0.572\times10^{-5}\Rightarrow\text{Sports}.$$

sections.title: Multinomial NB example 2: China?
sections.body:
Training: d1 "Chinese Beijing Chinese" (yes), d2 "Chinese Chinese Shanghai" (yes), d3 "Chinese Macao" (yes), d4 "Tokyo Japan Chinese" (no). Test d5 "Chinese Chinese Chinese Tokyo Japan". $N_{yes}(\text{Chinese})=5$, $N_{no}(\text{Chinese})=1$, $|V|=6$, words in Yes = 8, in No = 3 (p.67). $\hat P(w\mid C)=\frac{n_k(w)+1}{\sum_sn_k(w_s)+|V|}$.

$$\hat P(c)=\tfrac34,\ \hat P(\bar c)=\tfrac14;\quad \hat P(\text{Chinese}\mid c)=\tfrac{5+1}{8+6}=\tfrac37,\ \hat P(\text{Tokyo}\mid c)=\hat P(\text{Japan}\mid c)=\tfrac1{14};\quad \hat P(\text{Chinese}\mid\bar c)=\hat P(\text{Tokyo}\mid\bar c)=\hat P(\text{Japan}\mid\bar c)=\tfrac29.$$

$P(C_k\mid D)\propto P(C_k)\prod_{j=1}^{\text{len}(D)}P(u_j\mid C_k)$ over each word $u_j$ of the test document (p.69): $\hat P(c\mid d_5)\propto\frac34(\frac37)^3\frac1{14}\frac1{14}\approx0.0003$, $\hat P(\bar c\mid d_5)\propto\frac14(\frac29)^3\frac29\frac29\approx0.0001$ → China. Three occurrences of "Chinese" outweigh "Tokyo" and "Japan".

sections.title: Naïve Bayes summary model and variants
sections.body:
Model: joint distribution $P(X,Y)=P(Y)P(X\mid Y)$, $P(X=X_1..X_n,Y=y_k)=P(Y=y_k)P(X_1..X_n\mid Y=y_k)$. Learning: $P(Y)\sim\text{Ber}(p)$ (categorical for $K$ classes); for each attribute:

  • $P(X\mid Y)\sim\text{Ber}(\pi)$ → multivariate Bernoulli NB ($X_i$ binary; absent words count too).
  • $P(X\mid Y)\sim\text{Multinom}(\pi,n)$ → multinomial NB ($X_i$ counts, e.g. words).
  • $P(X\mid Y)\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ → Gaussian NB ($X_i$ real-valued).

sections.title: Logistic regression vs Naïve Bayes
sections.plain: Discriminative vs generative; GNB implies the logistic form.
sections.body: Naïve Bayes computes $P(Y\mid X)$ by learning $P(Y)$ and $P(X\mid Y)$: why not learn $P(Y\mid X)$ directly (p.71)? The parametric form of $P(Y\mid X)$ used by logistic regression is precisely the form implied by Gaussian NB assumptions (with class-independent variances) (p.72). Sketch: $$\log\frac{P(Y=1\mid x)}{P(Y=0\mid x)}=\log\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}+\sum_i\Big[\frac{\mu_{i1}-\mu_{i0}}{\sigma_i^2}x_i+\frac{\mu_{i0}^2-\mu_{i1}^2}{2\sigma_i^2}\Big],$$ linear in $x$, so $P(Y=1\mid x)=\sigma(w_0+\sum w_ix_i)$. LR is a closely related alternative to GNB, but they can produce different results: LR fits $w$ directly (better asymptotically when the NB assumption fails); GNB converges faster with little data (Ng & Jordan, 2002).

sections.title: Features of Bayesian learning
sections.body: Each observed example can incrementally decrease or increase the estimated probability that a hypothesis is correct, a more flexible approach than algorithms that completely eliminate a hypothesis inconsistent with a single example (p.73). Prior knowledge can be combined with data, hypotheses can make probabilistic predictions, and new instances can be classified by combining several hypotheses weighted by their probabilities.

sections.title: Practical issues
sections.plain: Needs many probabilities; Bayes optimal is costly.
sections.body: Bayesian methods require initial knowledge of many probabilities, often estimated from background knowledge, previously available data and assumptions about the form of distributions. Significant computational cost is required to determine the Bayes optimal hypothesis in general (linear in the number of candidate hypotheses) (p.74).

TypeGenerativeDiscriminativeInstance-based
Training$O(nd)$, one pass, closed form$O(nd)$ per iterationstore
ProbabilitiesOften over-confidentUsually well calibratedVote fractions
Small dataStrongNeeds moreWeak in high-d
Missing featuresEasy: drop the factorNeeds imputationNeeds imputation
  • "P(x | y) from a Gaussian is a probability." It is a density; compare densities only across classes at the same x.
  • "Laplace smoothing is always α = 1." α is a hyperparameter; tune it (often 0.01–1 for text).
  • "MLE is unbiased." The MLE of a Gaussian variance divides by n and is biased low.
  • "MAP is fully Bayesian." MAP is a point estimate; full Bayesian inference keeps the whole posterior (posterior predictive).

code.title: MLE and MAP worked examples
code.explain: The discrete-PMF MLE (θ = 0.5), Gaussian vs Laplace noise (least squares vs least absolute deviations), the continuous MAP example (x = 0.5) and the Bayes optimal classifier.
mistakes: Maximising the likelihood directly and underflowing; always use logs.
code.notes: With Laplace noise, LAD is the MLE and is more robust to outliers than OLS.
code.code:
# MLE and MAP worked examples from the session, checked numerically
import numpy as np
from fractions import Fraction as F

# 1) Discrete PMF: P(0)=2t/3, P(1)=t/3, P(2)=2(1-t)/3, P(3)=(1-t)/3
obs = [3, 0, 2, 1, 3, 2, 1, 0, 2, 1]
pmf = {0: lambda t: 2*t/3, 1: lambda t: t/3, 2: lambda t: 2*(1-t)/3, 3: lambda t: (1-t)/3}
grid = np.linspace(0.001, 0.999, 9999)
LL = sum(np.log(pmf[x](grid)) for x in obs)
print("counts:", {k: obs.count(k) for k in range(4)})
print("theta_MLE (grid) =", round(grid[LL.argmax()], 3), " closed form 5/10 =", 5/10)

# 2) Gaussian noise -> least squares; Laplace noise -> absolute error
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.uniform(0, 10, 200); y = 2 + 0.5*x + rng.laplace(0, 1, 200)
X = np.c_[np.ones_like(x), x]
ols = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]
from scipy.optimize import minimize
lad = minimize(lambda t: np.abs(y - X@t).sum(), ols, method="Nelder-Mead").x
print("OLS (Gaussian MLE):", ols.round(3), " LAD (Laplace MLE):", lad.round(3))
mu = X@lad; print("Laplace scale MLE = mean|y - mu| =", round(np.abs(y - mu).mean(), 3))

# 3) MAP: prior f(x)=2x on [0,1], likelihood p(y|x)=x(1-x)^(y-1), y=3
post = lambda t: t*(1-t)**2 * 2*t
for t in (0, 0.5, 1): print(f"posterior({t}) = {post(t):.3f}")
print("argmax on grid:", round(grid[post(grid).argmax()], 3))

# 4) Bayes optimal classifier vs MAP hypothesis
P_h = np.array([.4, .3, .3]); P_plus = np.array([1, 0, 0])
print("P(+|D) =", P_h@P_plus, " P(-|D) =", P_h@(1-P_plus), "-> Bayes optimal: -, MAP hypothesis h1 says +")

code.title: Naïve Bayes: tennis, Gaussian features, text
code.explain: Reproduces every Naïve Bayes number in the session, with and without Laplace smoothing, plus Gaussian and multinomial variants, and checks the text example with MultinomialNB.
mistakes: Smoothing with the wrong d (number of distinct values of that attribute, or vocabulary size for text).
code.notes: sklearn's GaussianNB uses the MLE (divide by n) variance plus a tiny var_smoothing term.
code.code:
# Naive Bayes worked examples: Play Tennis (with/without Laplace), Gaussian NB, text NB
import numpy as np
from math import prod, exp, sqrt, pi

cols = ["Sky", "AirTemp", "Humidity", "Wind", "Forecast"]
D = [("Sunny","Warm","Normal","Strong","Same","Yes"), ("Sunny","Warm","High","Strong","Same","No"),
     ("Rainy","Cold","High","Strong","Change","No"), ("Sunny","Warm","Normal","Breeze","Same","Yes"),
     ("Sunny","Hot","Normal","Breeze","Same","No"), ("Rainy","Cold","High","Strong","Change","No"),
     ("Sunny","Warm","High","Strong","Change","Yes")]
vals = [sorted({r[i] for r in D}) for i in range(5)]
def score(x, c, alpha=0):
    rows = [r for r in D if r[5] == c]; s = len(rows) / len(D)
    for i, v in enumerate(x):
        s *= (sum(r[i] == v for r in rows) + alpha) / (len(rows) + alpha * len(vals[i]))
    return s
for x in [("Sunny","Warm","Normal","Strong","Change"), ("Rainy","Warm","Normal","Breeze","Same")]:
    for a in (0, 1):
        y, n = score(x, "Yes", a), score(x, "No", a)
        print(x, "laplace" if a else "MLE    ", f"Yes={y:.5f} No={n:.5f} ->", "Yes" if y > n else "No")

# Gaussian NB on humidity (sample std, as on the slide)
hum = {"Yes": [85, 83, 85], "No": [80, 70, 90, 50]}
pdf = lambda x, m, s: exp(-(x-m)**2/(2*s*s)) / (s*sqrt(2*pi))
for c, v in hum.items():
    m, s = np.mean(v), np.std(v, ddof=1)
    print(f"humidity|{c}: mean={m:.2f} sd(ddof=1)={s:.2f} var={s*s:.2f}  N(60)={pdf(60, m, s):.3e}")
# slide 57: class-1 mean and (population) variance of X1
x1 = np.array([2, -1.2, 2.2]); print("X1|Y=1 mean", x1.mean(), "var", round(x1.var(), 2))

# Students: hours (Gaussian) + gender (categorical)
S = [(4.5,"M","Pass"), (7,"F","Pass"), (2,"M","Fail"), (4,"F","Fail"), (2.5,"M","Fail"), (3,"F","Fail"), (8.3,"M","Fail"), (8,"F","Pass"), (9,"M","Pass")]
for c in ("Pass", "Fail"):
    h = [r[0] for r in S if r[2] == c]; g = [r[1] for r in S if r[2] == c]
    for dd in (1, 0):
        m, s = np.mean(h), np.std(h, ddof=dd)
        print(f"{c}: prior={len(h)/9:.3f} mean={m:.3f} sd(ddof={dd})={s:.3f} N(3.5)={pdf(3.5, m, s):.4f} P(M)={g.count('M')}/{len(g)} score={len(h)/9*g.count('M')/len(g)*pdf(3.5, m, s):.4f}")

# Text NB (multinomial, Laplace)
docs = [("a great game","S"), ("the election was over","N"), ("very clean match","S"), ("a clean but forgettable game","S"), ("it was a close election","N")]
V = sorted({w for d, _ in docs for w in d.split()}); print("|V| =", len(V))
def text_score(s, c):
    words = [w for d, k in docs if k == c for w in d.split()]
    p = sum(k == c for _, k in docs) / len(docs)
    return p * prod((words.count(w) + 1) / (len(words) + len(V)) for w in s.split())
print("'a very close game': Sports", f"{text_score('a very close game','S'):.3e}", "Not", f"{text_score('a very close game','N'):.3e}")
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB
cv = CountVectorizer(token_pattern=r"(?u)\b\w+\b"); Xt = cv.fit_transform([d for d, _ in docs])
nb = MultinomialNB(alpha=1).fit(Xt, [k for _, k in docs]); print("sklearn:", nb.predict(cv.transform(["a very close game"]))[0])
# Chinese example (IR book)
P = {"c": 3/4 * (6/14)**3 * (1/14) * (1/14), "not c": 1/4 * (2/9)**3 * (2/9) * (2/9)}
print({k: round(v, 5) for k, v in P.items()})
